articles.description:
Short answer: use a Node.js chat completions API adapter to summarize text, then enforce a local schema gate before a moderation result enters the customer support review queue.
The constraint is structured output, not prose quality. A support moderation queue needs a decision that downstream code can trust: a category, a severity, a short rationale, and no extra fields that quietly change the contract.
My smallest useful design is a narrow Node.js adapter around a chat-completions-style endpoint, followed by local validation. The model may draft the summary. It does not define the queue contract.
For a human review queue, I would start with four fields: label, severity, summary, and needsHumanReview. The first two drive sorting. The third gives the reviewer context. The last makes the han…
articles.title: Node.js Chat Completions API: Summarize Text for Moderation Review Queues

The second time I ran my upload batch, I got the email I had been dreading. A channel had flagged my account for double-posting. Nothing had gone wrong with the art. Nothing had crashed. My pipeline had simply done its job twice, and now I was sitting there writing an apology to a stock platform over a batch of files I had already posted. articles.description:
The Silent Crisis in AI Agent Execution
As autonomous AI agents transition from experimental chat interfaces to operational infrastructure—executing database queries, issuing API requests, and managing cloud environments—a fundamental security vulnerability has emerged: the lack of non-repudiable tool execution chains.
When a multi-agent system issues a financial wire, executes a database migration, or modifies access control lists, traditional logging captures what happened, but cannot cryptographically prove who authorized it or whether the tool call payload was tampered with in transit.
In high-consequence enterprise environments, unverified tool execution creates three primary failure modes:
Indirect Prompt Injection Exploitation: Adversaries manipulate context documents to inject unau…

articles.description:
When WooCommerce shows "No shipping options were found," the instinct is to start changing settings. That usually makes it harder to know what fixed it. A better approach is to follow the same chain WooCommerce follows when it builds a shipping package.
Is shipping enabled for the destination country in the general settings?
Does a shipping zone match the country, state or postcode? Zones are read top to bottom and the first match wins.
Does that zone contain at least one enabled method?
Does the cart meet that method's own rules (free shipping minimum, valid cost formula)?
If any link fails, the rate list is empty. Each step below tests one link.
Under WooCommerce, Settings, Shipping, Shipping settings, enable debug mode. It shows which zones match the address in the cart calculator and b…

articles.description:
Two Packages, One 2 GB Server: Requirements.txt as Product Discipline


The first batch I ever ran twice returned 39 rejected CSVs in under a minute. Not because my art was bad. Because I had fat-fingered a header and then re-run the upload script, and every channel treated the second pass as a fresh submission. One mistake, a whole evening gone. That day I learned that the most expensive things in a product pipeline are not render times. They are the small, dumb, repeatable errors that a script should have made impossible.
This post is about that lesson, and about something that surprised me while cleaning up the kit built from that mess: the strongest proof of discipline in a pipeline is often a tiny requirements.txt.
The pipeline starter kit has four scripts. make_metadata.py builds upl…
articles.title: Two Packages, One 2 GB Server: Requirements.txt as Product Discipline

articles.author: Gowtham Potureddi
articles.description:
Designing a parking lot: the low-level design interview, explained


"Design a parking lot" is the most common opener in a low-level design interview, and it is deceptively easy to start and surprisingly easy to fail. The trap is treating it as a coding problem — there is no algorithm to crack and no test cases to pass. What the round is really testing is object-oriented design: can you turn a fuzzy real-world problem into a clean set of classes, draw the relationships between them, decide where behaviour lives, and keep the design open to change when the interviewer adds a requirement five minutes in? The parking lot is a favourite precisely because everyone understands the domain, so there is nowhere to hide — the whole conversation is about the quality of your model.
This guide walks th…
articles.title: Designing a parking lot: the low-level design interview, explained

SlothOps is a concept for a local AI project caretaker: a small developer tool that checks a repository and turns routine maintenance into a short, actionable report.
Instead of manually searching for TODOs, reviewing test output, and trying to remember what changed since the last session, SlothOps is designed to bring those signals together in one place.

Find TODO and FIXME comments.
Read Git status and recent commit history.
Run a user-approved test command and summarize its output.
Highlight likely maintenance tasks and suggest next steps.
Generate a concise project-health report.
The goal isn't to let an AI make unreviewed changes to…
